transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-17
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moran (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jon Wu (Redwood SE), Tom Castillo (CTO, Riverbend), Maya Patel (ML Lead), Derek Huang (Platform)

Summary:
Short intake focused on per-token economics and whether Riverbend should start on Redwood Hosted, move to Dedicated, or go Private (VPC/on-prem). Customer wants predictable monthly spend and latency SLO for synchronous chat (99th < 250ms). Lots of questions about batching, caching, and how caching interacts with PII.

Topics: pricing per token ranges, batching strategies, KV/prefix cache hit rates, dedicated capacity sizing, encryption/KMS & VPC requirements, pilot scope and benchmarks

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Moran: all right folks, thanks for joining, quick intro, i'm alex, ae at Redwood, we do inference platform hosting plus dedicated and private, uh Priya and jon are our SEs. Tom thanks for the invite.
[00:18] Tom Castillo: yeah thanks alex, i'll keep it short, we're trying to cost the chat assistant for Riverbend's support flows, need to decide hosted vs dedicated vs private, and want to understand unit economics and risk tradeoffs.
[00:28] Priya Nair: great. can you share current volume and typical token sizes? like average prompt/response lengths, concurrency, that kind of thing.
[00:33] Maya Patel: sure. average prompt is ~450 tokens, responses average 1.6k tokens, sessions are multi-turn but we count per-response more. Peak qps around 120 requests per second, sustained 60 qps.
[00:48] Derek Huang: and infra wise we run on k8s in AWS, need VPC peering for private deployments, can't route data through unknown third parties for some PII flows.
[00:58] Alex Moran: okay that's helpful. so rough unit econ: hosted per-token pricing varies by model; for a high-quality Llama-family variant you'd see in our buckets something like $0.0009 to $0.0014 per prompt token and lower for embeddings; but those numbers vary with quantized / batch optimized variants. also Dedicated flips to capacity-based pricing — predictable monthly commit + lower per-token egress.
[01:20] Tom Castillo: can you rephrase that, the per-token ranges — we're trying to model monthly spend for 2.5M responses.
[01:26] Jon Wu: sure — rough math: at 1.6k tokens per response, 2.5M responses is ~4B tokens. at $0.001/token that's $4M, at $0.0005/token $2M. but with batching and KV/prefix caching you can reduce effective tokens per response — e.g., prefix caching on repeated system prompts or long context pieces, can cut token bill by 15-40% depending on hit rate.
[01:48] Maya Patel: 15-40% is a big range. what's realistic for a support chat where we reuse a lot of boilerplate?
[01:54] Priya Nair: for support chat with templated context, i'd model 20-30% realistic hit rate for prefix cache and ~10-20% through response chunking and caching repeated embeddings. but it depends on session patterns. we'll need your prompt histograms.
[02:10] Derek Huang: what about batching impact on latency? our 99th p99 needs to be <250ms, can't really tolerate 500ms.
[02:15] Priya Nair: continuous batching reduces GPU waste — but it adds a small queuing delay. for low-latency targets we run smaller batch windows (e.g., 4-8 ms collection) and autoscale instances for concurrency; that usually keeps p99 within 200-300ms for gen models at moderate lengths. when going to Dedicated you can reserve inference pools to avoid noisy neighbor effects.
[02:38] Tom Castillo: what's the tradeoff of hosted vs dedicated for us? predictability is important — we hate surprise invoices.
[02:44] Alex Moran: Hosted is easiest to start, quick onboarding and transparent billing with dashboards. Dedicated gives committed monthly capacity with SLA-backed throughput and more predictable costs under commit. Private (VPC or on-prem) helps with compliance and residency but raises operational overhead and usually an up-front platform fee.
[03:02] Maya Patel: we have a compliance requirement for audit logs and KMS-managed keys for any PII handling. can hosted meet that?
[03:09] Jon Wu: hosted supports customer-managed keys via KMS integrations for encryption at rest, and we produce audit logs; for stricter needs we recommend Private (VPC) where you control the network and KMS. we can also support per-tenant log export. sometimes the docs refer to Redwood Privatee though, transcription's weird.
[03:28] Derek Huang: ok. one concrete ask — show us a pilot that runs our sample workload and gives us a unit econ spreadsheet that includes batching and cache knobs.
[03:36] Alex Moran: yes that's the typical pilot — we run a benchmark with your token histograms and QPS targets, test hosted and dedicated configs, and produce an expected monthly cost and per-1k-token number with sensitivity to cache hit rate.
[03:48] Tom Castillo: we also need to understand fallback behavior — if our dedicated pool is saturated do you fail over to hosted and what's the pricing for that?
[03:55] Priya Nair: we have routing policies — canary, fallback to lower-cost model variants, and cross-region fallbacks. fallback to hosted is possible with pre-authorized routing and you'll pay hosted rates for routed requests; Dedicated can be configured with burst capacity buffers. we'll include that in the pilot design.
[04:12] Maya Patel: a lot of vendors talk about quantization; do you have guidance on quality impact vs cost saving? we can't degrade accuracy for critical intents.
[04:21] Jon Wu: yes, quantization like 4-bit / int8 can cut runtime memory and cost significantly; but there are model-quality tradeoffs. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles per workload and we run evals on your prompt set to measure quality delta. many customers accept 4-bit for non-critical prompts and keep higher precision for critical scoring.
[04:40] Derek Huang: for private deployment, can we bring our own GPUs on-prem?
[04:44] Priya Nair: yes that's a supported pattern — hybrid private where control plane runs in our cloud but inference plane is in your DC with on-prem hardware. it requires some network setup and image certs. we'll document the operational needs.
[04:57] Tom Castillo: what's the SLA for latency and uptime if we go Dedicated?
[05:02] Alex Moran: SLA varies by contract tier, but we offer throughput/latency SLOs for Dedicated customers with credits for missed windows. we'll surface the exact numbers in the pilot contract.
[05:11] Maya Patel: ok, let's talk numbers — can you show a worked example: 120 peak qps, avg 1.6k tokens, 2.5M monthly responses, two scenarios: hosted only vs dedicated commit with 20% cache hit and 10% quantization saving?
[05:24] Jon Wu: sure, on the call i'll sketch it: hosted raw at $0.001/token -> $4M. with 20% cache hit effective tokens ~3.2B so $3.2M; with quantization savings maybe we can get to $2.9M. Dedicated commit prices are typically 20-40% lower per-token after commit and you get burst capacity; plus fixed monthly platform fee. exact depends on commit size.
[06:01] Tom Castillo: those deltas matter. We're evaluating budget bucket of $250k-500k/year for early pilot. everything above that needs exec signoff. can we scope a pilot that stays in that range?
[06:12] Alex Moran: yes — pilot typically is limited to a subset of traffic (e.g., 10% of production or a set of intents) to validate economics; we can run benchmarks to project full-run costs. pilot budget $50-150k is common.
[06:20] Maya Patel: what's the telemetry you provide during a pilot — token-level breakdown, cost per route, p99 latency?
[06:25] Priya Nair: Redwood Console gives per-route token counts, latency distributions, per-model costs, and we can expose tracing hooks. we'll share a sample dashboard.
[06:34] Derek Huang: about data retention — we need to ensure we can purge logs on request and maintain a 30-day retention max for certain tenants.
[06:41] Jon Wu: that's doable — hosted supports configurable retention policies and we can support short retention for regulated tenants; Private gives you full control.
[06:49] Tom Castillo: any gotchas on tokenization differences — like different tokenizers change our token counts?
[06:52] Priya Nair: yes tokenizers differ; we recommend running a local tokenization pass to normalize counts; we'll accept your histograms in our pilot harness to ensure alignment.
[07:02] Maya Patel: one more question — how do you charge for KV cache hits? do cached tokens still bill?
[07:06] Jon Wu: good question — cached KV/prefix tokens are not billed as new model inputs in our effective unit econ model; they reduce billable token counts because they avoid re-encoding or re-generation, though there may be small overhead for metadata. we'll show you the calculation in the spreadsheet.
[07:20] Tom Castillo: ok let's wrap with next steps.
[07:23] Alex Moran: action items summarized in the doc but to repeat: we need your token histograms and qps traces, we'll run a hosted benchmark and a dedicated baseline, produce a per-model per-1k-token sheet, and propose pilot scope to fit the $250k annualized runway cap.
[07:37] Maya Patel: sounds good, we'll share histograms and a sample session dump.
[07:41] Derek Huang: i'll pull K8s metrics and send link to dashboard.
[07:44] Tom Castillo: schedule the pilot kickoff for week of 9/29.

[54:30] Alex Moran: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and pilot plan; talk soon.

Notes on transcription: occasional mislabels and filler words; some product names may be misspelled in audio capture.

References shared during call: "pilot-scope-template.pdf" (link to be attached), "hosted-vs-dedicated-cost-sheet.xlsx" (to be shared), sample prompt histogram (customer to provide).

End of transcript.
